A drawing records what we can see. One drawing can show where a patch of sunlight falls on the classroom floor. To find out whether its position changes, we need to look again.

Over three school days, you will work with the same partner. Observe the patch at the beginning of the morning lesson and immediately after lunch each day. Your drawings will show where the visible light falls. They will not answer every question about why it is there.

Mark the outline of the light on the printed floor plan and write the time beside it. A pencil and ruler are provided. If part of the edge is fuzzy, mark it with a dotted line. A ruler can help you draw a straight line, but it cannot make the edge of the light clearer. If two groups mark an edge differently, compare what each group noticed before deciding whether either drawing needs to change.

Sometimes there may be no patch to see. Write “no patch visible” in the space for that observation and leave the floor plan unmarked. Do not draw yesterday’s patch in its place. You have recorded an observation, but you have not measured the patch’s position. The curtains will stay in their usual position. We will not control the clouds or record their thickness.

At the end, compare all six observation spaces with your partner. Write one sentence about a pattern your observations support and one question that remains. If you saw too few patches to establish a pattern, say so and explain which observations are missing. There is no particular pattern you have to find. A careful account of what you could not see can be more useful than a confident account of a patch nobody saw.

This release adds **Pause on Focus**, a new option in the desktop application’s Reading settings. By default, spoken image descriptions continue when you move keyboard focus to another control. Turn on Pause on Focus if you want the current description to stop when you move on.

Returning focus to the image will not resume the description. To hear it again from the beginning, use the existing Read Description command. “Pause” means speech stops while the saved description stays unchanged. Playback cannot resume at the word where it stopped.

Pause on Focus works with both automatic and manually requested descriptions. It does not turn on automatic image descriptions: if you previously turned them off, they will stay off after the update.

The option controls only descriptions spoken by the application. A separate screen reader controls its own speech, even when describing the same image, and audio inside a video remains controlled by the video player. You may therefore still hear speech or other audio after focus moves, especially if more than one source is playing. The mobile version keeps its existing behavior.

If a description continues after focus has visibly moved, please report it. If you can tell whether the speech came from the application or a separate screen reader, include that detail, but you do not need to identify the source to report the issue. response:
The pilot examined whether changing grate covers might reduce how long water remained above the pavement after rain. Six drains on two streets were observed during four storms before the change and four storms afterward. The three drains on the lower street received new covers, while the three on the upper street retained their existing covers. Crews had received more complaints about the lower street, which was why it was selected for the change. Cover allocation was therefore not random.

For each drain during each storm, a fixed camera recorded the number of minutes water remained above a painted reference line. A zero indicated no visible water above that line, not an absence of runoff. All 48 drain-storm observations were available. Across the 12 observations in each period on the lower street, the mean recorded duration fell from 18 minutes before the change to 10 minutes afterward. On the upper street, it fell from 9 minutes to 7 minutes. The lower street thus had a larger reduction: 8 minutes compared with 2 minutes. This difference may help guide further study, but it does not by itself establish an effect of the new covers.

Rainfall and cleaning complicate the comparison. The four later storms delivered less rain on average at the district gauge than the four earlier storms. Neither street had a rain gauge, and no measurements of rainfall intensity within storms were available. Crews also cleared accumulated leaves from all six drains on the day the covers were changed. Because the amount of debris present before cleaning was not recorded, cleaning cannot be assumed to explain the larger improvement on the lower street. Nor can its contribution be dismissed simply because both streets were cleaned.

The cameras documented shorter durations above the reference line at both sets of drains in the later period. Drainage capacity was not directly measured, and the pilot did not measure the number of flooded properties or collect property-damage observations. Peak water depth was not extracted from the images. A change in peak depth could matter even if the recorded duration stayed the same, so duration alone does not capture every potentially relevant change.

A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains and record local rainfall intensity and debris before cleaning. These measures could address some of the present ambiguities, although rotating covers would not make storms identical. The existing recordings remain useful for describing conditions during these eight storms and for assessing whether the camera-based duration measure is practical. Staff reported that all recordings could be scored, but agreement between different scorers has not been tested.

## Design and data

We observed six drains on two streets during four storms before a cover change and four storms after it. Covers were changed at the three drains on the lower street. The three drains on the upper street kept their covers. The lower street was chosen because crews had received more complaints there, so cover allocation was not random.

On the upper street, it fell from 9 minutes to 7 minutes. The reduction was larger on the street where covers changed. This difference may help decide what to study next, but the comparison alone does not identify a cover effect.

## Other differences between the periods

Three other differences between the periods could account for some of the change.

- **Rainfall.** The four later storms delivered less rain on average at the district gauge. No gauge was installed on either street, and the report has no within-storm intensity measurements.

- Whether the cover change affected drainage capacity or property flooding.
- Whether peak water depth changed.

A later study could rotate covers among comparable drains and record local rainfall intensity and debris before cleaning. This would address some of the present ambiguities, although rotation alone would not make storms identical.

Four classes compared two worksheet layouts during one lesson. Both versions asked pupils to explain why the same amount of water looks different in a tall vessel and a wide vessel. Version A placed a diagram beside each question. Version B grouped the same diagrams on a reference page. The wording, diagrams, and question order were otherwise identical. The analysis included 52 returned worksheets for A and 49 for B. Six additional pupils assigned A and five assigned B were absent. Only returned worksheets were analysed. We should install the two proposed automatic warning signs because the underpass sometimes fills with water before a maintenance crew can close the road. Approval should depend on naming a team responsible for monthly sensor checks, allocating staff time for those checks, and providing a manual road-closure procedure for when the system is unavailable. Staff time has not yet been allocated, so the purchase is not ready for approval.

The signs would address delayed warnings. They would not keep water out of the underpass or resolve the drainage problem. Installing them would complete the warning project, while the drainage project would remain unresolved.

Installing the signs is estimated to cost 18,000 units of local currency, compared with 140,000 for replacing the drainage pipe. Neither estimate includes annual maintenance. The signs have a lower initial cost, but we have no agreed estimate of how much either option would reduce injuries or vehicle damage. We should therefore assess the signs as a response to delayed warnings, not as a cheaper way to achieve the same result as pipe replacement.

The signs would activate when a water-level sensor crosses a set threshold. The sensor can fail, and the signs need power, so a dark sign cannot safely indicate that the road is clear. I propose adding a separate table of excluded runs to the report template and showing the number of runs attempted and retained beside the reported mean. The final summary currently lists only the runs used to calculate the mean. This makes the mean easy to read, but readers cannot tell whether there were no exclusions or whether exclusions were left out of the summary. The table would account for the difference between attempted and retained runs without adding excluded readings to the mean.

The proposal would document how we apply the existing exclusion rule, not change it. That rule excludes controller failures and retains unusual completed results unless a separately recorded equipment or handling fault justifies exclusion. For example, a run stopped because the temperature controller failed did not meet the stated measurement conditions. A completed run with an unusual result is different: the result alone does not establish that those conditions failed.

The proposed table would list each excluded run’s identifier, completion status, reason for exclusion, and whether a usable reading exists. It should be labeled as a record of exclusions. Raw readings would remain in the underlying record, available through the existing review process. Including every raw reading in the table is unnecessary for explaining the exclusion decisions and could make those decisions harder to see.

Each excluded run should appear even if it produced no usable reading. A table limited to excluded numeric values would omit those failures and could make a difficult batch look cleaner than it was. Reporting attempted and retained counts would make those failures visible without treating stopped runs as measured outcomes.

Showing excluded runs may invite readers to calculate a new mean from everything listed. Clear labeling would address that concern, but the risk remains. Reviewers would also still need to judge whether the documented reasons are convincing. A fuller table makes decisions available for inspection, but it cannot guarantee honest recording or resolve an ambiguous rule.

The additional reporting takes time, especially when the same fault affects several runs. We could permit a shared explanation for such a group, provided every affected run appears and is linked to that explanation. No reason should be omitted merely because it is repetitive. This would reduce repeated prose while preserving a countable record of the batch, though the tradeoff between fuller reporting and the work it requires would remain.

This makes the mean easy to read, but readers cannot tell whether a batch had no exclusions or whether excluded runs were simply omitted from the summary. The table would document exclusions without changing which readings enter the mean.

Our existing rule excludes runs stopped by controller failures and retains unusual completed results unless a separately recorded equipment or handling fault justifies exclusion. These cases differ because a controller failure means the stated measurement conditions were not met, whereas an unusual result alone does not establish that those conditions failed. The proposed table would let readers inspect how this rule was applied.

For each excluded run, I propose listing the run identifier, completion status, reason for exclusion, and whether a usable reading exists. The table should be labeled as a record of exclusions. It need not include raw readings, which would remain in the underlying record and be available through the existing review process. Including every raw reading could obscure the exclusion decisions and invite readers to calculate a new mean from everything shown. Labeling the table may help, but the risk of misinterpretation remains.

The table should include excluded runs even when they produced no usable reading. A table limited to excluded numeric values would omit those failures and could make a difficult batch look cleaner than it was. At the same time, stopped runs should not be counted as measured outcomes. I therefore propose reporting the number of runs attempted and the number retained beside the mean, with the exclusions table accounting for the difference.

This reporting would make exclusion decisions available for inspection, but reviewers would still need to judge whether the reasons are convincing. A fuller table cannot guarantee honest recording or repair an ambiguous rule. It also takes time to prepare, especially when the same fault affects several runs. We could permit a shared explanation for such a group, provided each affected run still appears and its reason is clear. That would reduce repetition while preserving a count of all runs, though the added reporting burden would remain.

**Proposal: report excluded runs in the report template**

The template would change in three ways:

1. The final summary reports the number of runs attempted and the number retained beside the mean.
2. A separate table, labeled as a record of exclusions, lists every excluded run with columns for run identifier, completion status, reason, and whether a usable reading exists.
3. When one fault affects several runs, the table may give a single shared explanation for the group, but each affected run still gets its own row.

The exclusion rule itself does not change. Controller failures are excluded, and unusual completed results are retained unless a separately recorded equipment or handling fault justifies excluding them. No excluded reading would enter the mean.

**Why the summary needs this**

The final summary now lists only the runs used to calculate the mean. A reader cannot tell whether a batch had no exclusions or whether the exclusions were dropped from the summary. The table, together with the attempted and retained counts, makes the difference visible.

The table would show how the existing rule was applied. A run stopped because the temperature controller failed did not meet the stated measurement conditions. A completed run with an unusual result is different, because an unusual result alone does not show that the conditions failed. A reader can check each exclusion against that distinction only if the exclusions are listed with reasons.

**Why the table has these columns**

Raw readings are left out because they are unnecessary for showing the decisions and would make the decisions harder to see. They stay in the underlying record and remain available through the existing review process.

The "usable reading exists" column and the attempted count are there because some runs produce no usable reading. A table of excluded numeric values would miss those runs and could make a difficult batch look cleaner than it was. Counting stopped runs as measured outcomes would distort the batch in the opposite way. Reporting attempted and retained counts beside the mean, with the table accounting for the difference, avoids both.

**What remains unsettled**

- Readers may use the table to calculate a new mean from every run listed. The labeling and the complete reasons are meant to discourage this, but they cannot prevent it.
- The table cannot guarantee honest recording or repair an ambiguous rule. Reviewers will still have to judge whether the documented reasons are convincing. The table only makes the decisions available for inspection.
- The extra reporting takes time, especially when the same fault affects several runs. The shared explanation reduces repeated prose while keeping the batch's history countable. Whether the added effort is worth the added inspectability is the question for the meeting.

The report template would add a separate table of excluded runs. The existing exclusion rule would not change. The proposal has three parts:

1. The table lists every excluded run with its run identifier, completion status, reason for exclusion, and whether a usable reading exists. It is labeled as a record of exclusions. It does not include raw readings, which stay in the underlying record and remain available through the existing review process.
2. The summary reports the number of runs attempted and the number retained beside the mean. The exclusions table accounts for the difference.
3. When one fault affects several runs, the table may give a single shared explanation for the group, but each affected run still gets its own row.

The final summary currently lists only the runs used to calculate the reported mean. That is convenient for reading the mean, but a reader cannot tell whether a batch had no exclusions or whether the exclusions simply disappeared from the summary. The table makes that visible. I am not proposing that excluded readings enter the mean.

The table shows how the existing rule was applied. That rule treats two cases differently. A run stopped because the temperature controller failed did not meet the stated measurement conditions. A completed run with an unusual result has not failed those conditions on that basis alone. The rule therefore excludes controller failures and retains unusual completed results, unless a separately recorded equipment or handling fault justifies excluding one.

**Why the table lists runs rather than readings**

A table of only excluded numeric values would miss runs with no usable reading, and that could make a difficult batch look cleaner than it was. Listing runs, with a column for whether a usable reading exists, covers those failures. Adding every raw reading would not serve this purpose and could make the decisions harder to see. Counting all stopped runs as measured outcomes would distort the results in the other direction, which is why the summary reports attempted and retained counts instead.

Allowing a shared explanation reduces repeated prose while keeping the batch's history countable, but it does not remove the work of listing each run. response:
**Claim.** On a finite probability space, let \(X\) be a real-valued reading and let \(G_1,\ldots,G_m\) partition the space into batch cells. Write \(p_j=\mathbb P(G_j)\), and define
\[
\mu_j=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle \frac{1}{p_j}\sum_{\omega\in G_j}\mathbb P(\{\omega\})X(\omega),&p_j>0,\\[6pt]
0,&p_j=0.
\end{cases}
\]
Let \(M=\mu_j\) on \(G_j\). Then, for every real constant \(c\),
\[
\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]
=\mathbb E[(X-M)^2]+\mathbb E[(M-c)^2].
\]
Consequently,
\[
\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]\geq \mathbb E[(X-M)^2],
\]
with equality exactly when \(M=c\) with probability one.

**Proof.** On each cell with \(p_j>0\), \(M\) is the conditional mean of \(X\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{\omega\in G_j}\mathbb P(\{\omega\})
\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr)
&=\sum_{\omega\in G_j}\mathbb P(\{\omega\})X(\omega)-p_j\mu_j\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(p_j=0\), every point in \(G_j\) has probability zero, so the same sum is zero.

Since \(M-c\) is constant on each cell, we can factor it out of the corresponding sum:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(X-M)(M-c)]
&=\sum_{j=1}^m(\mu_j-c)
\sum_{\omega\in G_j}\mathbb P(\{\omega\})
\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr)\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
This uses the zero conditional mean of the residual, without requiring independence.

Now expand pointwise:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(X-c)^2
&=\bigl((X-M)+(M-c)\bigr)^2\\
&=(X-M)^2+2(X-M)(M-c)+(M-c)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking expectations and using the vanishing cross term gives the identity. Finally,
\[
\mathbb E[(M-c)^2]=\sum_{j=1}^m p_j(\mu_j-c)^2\geq 0.
\]
This sum is zero exactly when \(\mu_j=c\) for every cell with \(p_j>0\). Cells with \(p_j=0\) impose no restriction, so this is equivalent to \(M=c\) with probability one. \(\square\)

**Claim.** On a finite probability space, let \(X\) be real-valued and let \(G_1,\ldots,G_m\) be a partition into batch cells. Write \(p_j=\mathbb P(G_j)\) and define
\[
\mu_j=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle \frac{1}{p_j}\sum_{\omega\in G_j}\mathbb P(\{\omega\})X(\omega),&p_j>0,\\[6pt]
0,&p_j=0.
\end{cases}
\]
Let \(M=\mu_j\) on \(G_j\). Then, for every real constant \(c\),
\[
\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]
=\mathbb E[(X-M)^2]+\mathbb E[(M-c)^2].
\]
Consequently,
\[
\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]\geq\mathbb E[(X-M)^2],
\]
with equality exactly when \(M=c\) with probability one.

**Proof.** On each cell with \(p_j>0\), the definition of \(\mu_j\) gives
\[
\mathbb E[X-M\mid G_j]
=\frac{1}{p_j}\sum_{\omega\in G_j}
\mathbb P(\{\omega\})\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr)
=0.
\]
Because \(M-c\) is constant on that cell, we can factor it out of the corresponding finite sum. If \(p_j=0\), every point in \(G_j\) has probability zero, so the cell contributes zero without requiring a conditional mean. Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(X-M)(M-c)]
&=\sum_{j=1}^m(\mu_j-c)
  \sum_{\omega\in G_j}\mathbb P(\{\omega\})
  \bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr)\\
&=\sum_{j:p_j>0}(\mu_j-c)p_j\,
  \mathbb E[X-M\mid G_j]\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]

Now expand pointwise:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(X-c)^2
&=\bigl((X-M)+(M-c)\bigr)^2\\
&=(X-M)^2+2(X-M)(M-c)+(M-c)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking expectations and using the vanishing cross term proves the identity.

Finally,
\[
\mathbb E[(M-c)^2]
=\sum_{j=1}^m p_j(\mu_j-c)^2\geq0.
\]
This sum is zero exactly when \(\mu_j=c\) for every cell with \(p_j>0\). The cells with \(p_j=0\) impose no condition, so equality holds exactly when \(M=c\) with probability one. \(\square\)

**Claim.** On a finite probability space, let $X$ be a real-valued reading, and let $G_1,\dots,G_m$ be a partition of the space into batch cells. For $p_j=P(G_j)>0$, define
$$\mu_j=\frac{\sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\{\omega\})X(\omega)}{p_j}.$$
Set $\mu_j=0$ when $p_j=0$, and let $M$ equal $\mu_j$ on $G_j$. Then for every real constant $c$,
$$E[(X-c)^2]=E[(X-M)^2]+E[(M-c)^2].$$
Consequently, $E[(X-c)^2]\ge E[(X-M)^2]$, with equality exactly when $M=c$ with probability one.

**Proof.** The space is finite, so every expectation is a finite sum: $E[Z]=\sum_\omega P(\{\omega\})Z(\omega)$. We show first that the cross term vanishes, then expand, then analyze the equality case.

*Step 1: The cross term vanishes.* On each cell $G_j$, $M$ takes the constant value $\mu_j$, so
$$M-c=\sum_{j=1}^m(\mu_j-c)\,\mathbf 1_{G_j}.$$
Multiplying by $X-M$ and taking expectations gives
$$
E[(X-M)(M-c)]
=\sum_{j=1}^m(\mu_j-c)\,E[(X-M)\mathbf 1_{G_j}]
=\sum_{j=1}^m(\mu_j-c)\sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\{\omega\})\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr).
$$
We show that each inner sum is zero.

- If $p_j>0$, the definition of $\mu_j$ gives $\sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\{\omega\})X(\omega)=p_j\mu_j$. Since $\sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\{\omega\})=p_j$,
$$
\sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\{\omega\})\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr)
=p_j\mu_j-\mu_j p_j=0.
$$
- If $p_j=0$, each probability $P(\{\omega\})$ with $\omega\in G_j$ is nonnegative, and these values sum to $0$. Hence $P(\{\omega\})=0$ for every $\omega\in G_j$, so every term of the inner sum is zero. The value $\mu_j=0$ assigned to this cell plays no role.

Therefore $E[(X-M)(M-c)]=0$. This step uses only the finite sums and the definition of $\mu_j$. It does not assume that $X-M$ and $M$ are independent, and it does not need independence.

*Step 2: The identity.* Pointwise, $X-c=(X-M)+(M-c)$, so
$$
(X-c)^2=(X-M)^2+2(X-M)(M-c)+(M-c)^2.
$$
Taking expectations and using Step 1,
$$
E[(X-c)^2]=E[(X-M)^2]+2\cdot 0+E[(M-c)^2]=E[(X-M)^2]+E[(M-c)^2].
$$

*Step 3: The inequality.* The term $E[(M-c)^2]=\sum_\omega P(\{\omega\})\bigl(M(\omega)-c\bigr)^2$ is a sum of nonnegative terms, so it is at least $0$. Hence $E[(X-c)^2]\ge E[(X-M)^2]$.

*Step 4: The equality condition.* A finite sum of nonnegative terms is zero exactly when each term is zero. So $E[(M-c)^2]=0$ if and only if $P(\{\omega\})\bigl(M(\omega)-c\bigr)^2=0$ for every $\omega$. This holds if and only if $M(\omega)=c$ for every $\omega$ with $P(\{\omega\})>0$. Equivalently,
$$
P(M\neq c)=\sum_{\omega:\,M(\omega)\neq c}P(\{\omega\})=0,
$$
which is the statement that $M=c$ with probability one.

The qualifier "with probability one" is needed here. A cell with $p_j=0$ has $\mu_j=0$, so $M=0$ on that cell. If $c\neq 0$, then $M\neq c$ on that cell, yet its probability is zero, so it contributes nothing to either side of the identity. The points of probability zero are exactly where $M$ may differ from $c$ without affecting the equality. $\blacksquare$

**Claim.** Let $(\Omega,P)$ be a finite probability space, let $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and let $G_1,\dots,G_m$ be a partition of $\Omega$. Put $p_j=P(G_j)$ and define

$$
\mu_j=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{p_j}\displaystyle\sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\{\omega\})X(\omega), & p_j>0,\\[2ex] 0, & p_j=0.\end{cases}
$$

Let $M(\omega)=\mu_j$ for $\omega\in G_j$. Then for every real constant $c$,

$$
E[(X-c)^2]=E[(X-M)^2]+E[(M-c)^2].
$$

Consequently $E[(X-c)^2]\ge E[(X-M)^2]$, with equality if and only if $P(M=c)=1$.

**Proof.** On a finite space, $E[Y]=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}P(\{\omega\})Y(\omega)$, a finite sum. All expectations below exist, and linearity applies without restriction. For any $Y$ and any cell $G_j$,

$$
E[Y\mathbf 1_{G_j}]=\sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\{\omega\})Y(\omega).
$$

*Step 1: each cell has zero conditional mean.* We show that for every $j$,

$$
E[(X-M)\mathbf 1_{G_j}]=0. \tag{1}
$$

If $p_j>0$, then $M=\mu_j$ on $G_j$, so

$$
E[(X-M)\mathbf 1_{G_j}]
=\sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\{\omega\})X(\omega)-\mu_j\sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\{\omega\})
=p_j\mu_j-\mu_jp_j=0,
$$

where the first sum equals $p_j\mu_j$ by the definition of $\mu_j$. This says that the conditional mean of $X-M$ given $G_j$ is zero.

If $p_j=0$, then $P(\{\omega\})=0$ for every $\omega\in G_j$, because the probabilities are nonnegative and sum to $p_j$. Every term in the sum is zero, so (1) holds.

*Step 2: the cross term vanishes.* Since the cells partition $\Omega$,

$$
M-c=\sum_{j=1}^m(\mu_j-c)\mathbf 1_{G_j}.
$$

Each $\mu_j-c$ is a constant, so

$$
E[(X-M)(M-c)]=\sum_{j=1}^m(\mu_j-c)\,E[(X-M)\mathbf 1_{G_j}]=0
$$

by (1). This step uses only the fact that $M-c$ is constant on each cell. It does not assert that $X-M$ and $M$ are independent.

*Step 3: the identity.* Pointwise, $X-c=(X-M)+(M-c)$, so

$$
(X-c)^2=(X-M)^2+2(X-M)(M-c)+(M-c)^2.
$$

Taking expectations and applying Step 2 gives

$$
E[(X-c)^2]=E[(X-M)^2]+2E[(X-M)(M-c)]+E[(M-c)^2]=E[(X-M)^2]+E[(M-c)^2].
$$

*Step 4: the inequality and the equality case.* Since $E[(M-c)^2]\ge 0$, we get $E[(X-c)^2]\ge E[(X-M)^2]$. Equality holds exactly when $E[(M-c)^2]=0$.

Because $M-c$ equals $\mu_j-c$ on $G_j$,

$$
E[(M-c)^2]=\sum_{j=1}^m p_j(\mu_j-c)^2,
$$

a sum of nonnegative terms. It vanishes if and only if $p_j(\mu_j-c)^2=0$ for every $j$. That is, every cell with $p_j>0$ has $\mu_j=c$. Cells with $p_j=0$ contribute nothing, whatever their value of $\mu_j$. Therefore

$$
P(M\ne c)=\sum_{j:\,\mu_j\ne c}p_j=0
$$

exactly when $E[(M-c)^2]=0$. So equality holds if and only if $P(M=c)=1$.

*Remark on zero-probability cells.* Such cells enter the proof in Step 1, where each term of their sum is zero, and in Step 4, where their weight $p_j$ is zero. They do not contribute to any expectation. Their value $\mu_j=0$ is a convention, so $M=c$ holds only up to a null set, not necessarily on all of $\Omega$. The proof uses no independence assumption.

\[

 +2\mathbb E[(X-M)(M-c)]
 +\mathbb E[(M-c)^2]\\

\]

**Proof.** Every expectation is a finite sum over $\Omega$. Write $\mathbb E[Y]=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}P(\{\omega\})Y(\omega)$. The cells $G_1,\dots,G_m$ are disjoint and cover $\Omega$, so any such sum can be split as a sum over cells.

**Pointwise expansion.** Fix a real constant $c$. Since $X-c=(X-M)+(M-c)$, at each $\omega$

$$
(X-c)^2=(X-M)^2+2(X-M)(M-c)+(M-c)^2 .
$$

Taking expectations, which is linear on a finite space, gives

$$
\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]=\mathbb E[(X-M)^2]+2\,\mathbb E[(X-M)(M-c)]+\mathbb E[(M-c)^2]. \tag{1}
$$

It remains to show that the cross term is zero.

**The cross term vanishes.** We split the sum by cells. On $G_j$ the function $M$ equals the constant $\mu_j$, so $M-c=\mu_j-c$ can be taken out of the inner sum:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(X-M)(M-c)]
&=\sum_{j=1}^m\ \sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\{\omega\})\,\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr)(\mu_j-c)\\
&=\sum_{j=1}^m(\mu_j-c)\,S_j,
\qquad S_j:=\sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\{\omega\})\bigl(X(\omega)-\mu_j\bigr).
\end{aligned}
$$

We show $S_j=0$ for every $j$, in two cases.

*Case $p_j>0$.* By the definition of $\mu_j$, $\sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\{\omega\})X(\omega)=p_j\mu_j$. Also $\sum_{\omega\in G_j}P(\{\omega\})\mu_j=p_j\mu_j$. Hence

$$
S_j=p_j\mu_j-p_j\mu_j=0 .
$$

This is the statement that the residual $X-M$ has conditional mean zero on $G_j$. Only this fact is used, and no independence between $X-M$ and $M$ is needed. The factor $\mu_j-c$ is a constant on $G_j$, so it multiplies the cell sum $S_j$ and does not interact with it.

*Case $p_j=0$.* Here $\mu_j=0$ by convention, but the value is irrelevant. Each $P(\{\omega\})$ with $\omega\in G_j$ is nonnegative, and these terms sum to $p_j=0$, so $P(\{\omega\})=0$ for every $\omega\in G_j$. Every term of $S_j$ therefore contains the factor $P(\{\omega\})=0$, and $S_j=0$. This is where the zero-probability cells enter. The conditional mean is undefined there, but the cell contributes nothing to the sum.

Since $S_j=0$ for all $j$, the cross term is zero:

$$
\mathbb E[(X-M)(M-c)]=\sum_{j=1}^m(\mu_j-c)\cdot 0=0 .
$$

**The identity.** Substituting this into (1) gives

$$
\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]=\mathbb E[(X-M)^2]+\mathbb E[(M-c)^2].
$$

**The inequality and its equality case.** Since $(M-c)^2\ge 0$ pointwise, $\mathbb E[(M-c)^2]\ge 0$, so

$$
\mathbb E[(X-c)^2]\ge\mathbb E[(X-M)^2].
$$

By the identity, equality holds exactly when $\mathbb E[(M-c)^2]=0$. Grouping this sum by cells,

$$
\mathbb E[(M-c)^2]=\sum_{j=1}^m p_j(\mu_j-c)^2 .
$$

Every term is nonnegative, so the sum is zero exactly when $p_j(\mu_j-c)^2=0$ for each $j$. For a cell with $p_j>0$ this means $\mu_j=c$. For a cell with $p_j=0$ the term is zero whatever $\mu_j$ is, so the convention $\mu_j=0$ puts no restriction on $c$. Equality therefore holds exactly when $\mu_j=c$ on every cell of positive probability. The event $\{M\ne c\}$ is the union of the cells with $\mu_j\ne c$. When equality holds, these cells all have $p_j=0$, so $P(M\ne c)=0$. Conversely, if $P(M\ne c)=0$, every cell with $\mu_j\ne c$ has probability zero, so every term above vanishes. **Claim.** Let \(P\) be a real \(d\times d\) matrix, where \(d\geq 1\), satisfying
\[
P^2=P,\qquad P^T=P.
\]
Let
\[
S=\{Pz:z\in\mathbb R^d\}
\]
be the subspace of permitted layout displacements. For every \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), the unique \(y\in S\) minimizing \(\|x-y\|^2\) is \(Px\). More precisely, for every \(y\in S\),
\[
\|x-y\|^2=\|x-Px\|^2+\|Px-y\|^2,
\]
where \(\|v\|^2=v^Tv\).

**Proof.** Fix \(x\in\mathbb R^d\). The vector \(Px\) belongs to \(S\) by definition. The hypothesis \(P^2=P\) means that applying \(P\) again leaves every vector in \(S\) unchanged: if \(y=Pz\), then
\[
Py=P(Pz)=P^2z=Pz=y.
\]
In particular, \(P(Px)=Px\). By linearity,
\[
P(Px-y)=P(Px)-Py=Px-y.
\]
The same hypothesis shows that \(P\) sends the residual \(x-Px\) to zero:
\[
P(x-Px)=Px-P^2x=Px-Px=0.
\]

We now use the symmetry hypothesis \(P^T=P\) to show that the residual is perpendicular to \(Px-y\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
(x-Px)^T(Px-y)
&=(x-Px)^TP(Px-y)\\
&=\bigl(P(x-Px)\bigr)^T(Px-y)\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
The first equality uses \(P(Px-y)=Px-y\). For the second, symmetry gives
\[
\bigl(P(x-Px)\bigr)^T=(x-Px)^TP^T=(x-Px)^TP.
\]
The last equality uses \(P(x-Px)=0\).

Since
\[
x-y=(x-Px)+(Px-y),
\]
expanding the squared Euclidean norm gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|x-y\|^2
&=\|x-Px\|^2
  +2(x-Px)^T(Px-y)
  +\|Px-y\|^2\\
&=\|x-Px\|^2+\|Px-y\|^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
The cross term is zero by the calculation above.

The first term does not depend on \(y\), and the second is nonnegative. Choosing \(y=Px\) makes the second term zero, so \(Px\) attains the minimum. Any other minimizer must also satisfy
\[
\|Px-y\|^2=0.
\]
A Euclidean norm is zero only for the zero vector, so \(y=Px\). Thus the minimizer is unique.

This includes the zero-dimensional case: when \(P=0\), we have \(S=\{0\}\), and the identity reduces to \(\|x\|^2=\|x\|^2+0\). When \(P=I\), we have \(S=\mathbb R^d\) and \(x-Px=0\). The conclusion concerns squared distance to the fixed subspace \(S\), rather than arbitrary layout constraints.

**Claim.** Let $P\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ with $d\ge 1$ satisfy $P^2=P$ and $P^\top=P$. Let

$$
S=\{Pz : z\in\mathbb R^d\}
$$

be the set of permitted layout displacements. For every $x\in\mathbb R^d$, the squared distance $\|x-y\|^2$ over $y\in S$ has a unique minimizer, namely $y=Px$. More precisely, for every $y\in S$,

$$
\|x-y\|^2=\|x-Px\|^2+\|Px-y\|^2. \tag{1}
$$

Here $\|v\|^2=v^\top v$.

**Proof.**

*Step 1: Vectors in $S$ are fixed by $P$.* Since $Px\in S$ by definition, take $z=x$. For any $y\in S$, write $y=Pz$. Then

$$
Py=P^2z=Pz=y,
$$

where the middle equality uses $P^2=P$. Applying this to $Px\in S$ gives $P(Px)=Px$. Therefore, for any $y\in S$, both $Px$ and $y$ are fixed by $P$, and

$$
P(Px-y)=P(Px)-Py=Px-y. \tag{2}
$$

*Step 2: $P$ annihilates the residual.* Using $P^2=P$,

$$
P(x-Px)=Px-P^2x=0. \tag{3}
$$

*Step 3: The residual is orthogonal to $S$ displacements.* For $y\in S$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
(x-Px)^\top(Px-y)
&=(x-Px)^\top P(Px-y) &&\text{by (2)}\\
&=\big(P^\top(x-Px)\big)^\top(Px-y) &&\text{by the rule } a^\top Pb=(P^\top a)^\top b\\
&=\big(P(x-Px)\big)^\top(Px-y) &&\text{by } P^\top=P\\
&=0 &&\text{by (3)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Symmetry is used only in the third line. The idempotence $P^2=P$ is used in (2) and (3).

*Step 4: Expansion.* Write $x-y=(x-Px)+(Px-y)$. Expanding the squared norm gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\|x-y\|^2
&=\|x-Px\|^2+2\,(x-Px)^\top(Px-y)+\|Px-y\|^2\\
&=\|x-Px\|^2+\|Px-y\|^2,
\end{aligned}
$$

where the cross term vanishes by Step 3. This establishes (1) for every $y\in S$.

*Step 5: Minimizer and uniqueness.* The first term on the right of (1) does not depend on $y$. The second term is a squared norm, so it is nonnegative. Hence

$$
\|x-y\|^2\ge\|x-Px\|^2\quad\text{for all }y\in S.
$$

Taking $y=Px\in S$ makes $\|Px-y\|^2=0$, so equality holds and $Px$ attains the minimum. Now suppose $y\in S$ also attains this minimum value. Then (1) gives $\|Px-y\|^2=0$. A squared Euclidean norm is zero only at the zero vector, so $y=Px$. Thus the minimizer is unique.

*Step 6: Boundary cases.* The argument covers every $d\ge 1$ and every $P$ satisfying the two hypotheses.

- If $P=0$, then $S=\{0\}$, which is the zero-dimensional permitted subspace. The minimizer is $0=Px$ for every $x$, and (1) still holds, since the proof never uses a dimension count.
- If $P=I$, then $S=\mathbb R^d$ and $Px=x$. The residual $x-Px$ is zero, so the minimum value is $0$.

*Scope.* The proof uses only $P^2=P$ and $P^\top=P$. It does not assume that $P$ is invertible or that $P$ has any particular rank. The conclusion concerns the squared distance from $x$ to the fixed set $S$. It does not address other possible layout constraints.

**Claim.** Let $P$ be a real $d\times d$ matrix with $d\ge 1$, $P^2=P$ and $P^T=P$. Let $S=\{Pz : z\in\mathbb R^d\}$ be the set of permitted layout displacements, and write $\|v\|^2=v^Tv$. Then for every $x\in\mathbb R^d$ and every $y\in S$,

$$
\|x-y\|^2=\|x-Px\|^2+\|Px-y\|^2 .
$$

Consequently $Px$ is the unique element of $S$ that minimizes $\|x-y\|^2$.

**Proof.** Fix $x\in\mathbb R^d$ and $y\in S$, and write $y=Pz$.

*Step 1: $Px\in S$, and $P$ fixes every element of $S$.* Taking $z=x$ shows $Px\in S$. For any element $Pz$ of $S$, idempotence gives

$$
P(Pz)=P^2z=Pz .
$$

Applying this to $Px$ and to $y$ gives $P(Px)=Px$ and $Py=y$. Hence the vector $w:=Px-y$ satisfies

$$
Pw=P(Px)-Py=Px-y=w .
$$

*Step 2: the residual is killed by $P$.* Let $r:=x-Px$. Then

$$
Pr=Px-P^2x=Px-Px=0 .
$$

*Step 3: the cross term vanishes.* Using $w=Pw$ from Step 1, then symmetry of $P$ to move $P$ onto $r$, then $Pr=0$ from Step 2:

$$
\begin{aligned}
r^Tw
&=r^T(Pw)\\
&=(P^Tr)^Tw\\
&=(Pr)^Tw\\
&=0 .
\end{aligned}
$$

The second line is the identity $r^TP=(P^Tr)^T$, and the third replaces $P^T$ by $P$.

*Step 4: the identity.* Since $x-y=r+w$,

$$
\|x-y\|^2=(r+w)^T(r+w)=r^Tr+2\,r^Tw+w^Tw=\|r\|^2+\|w\|^2 ,
$$

where $w^Tr=r^Tw$ because both are scalars, and $r^Tw=0$ by Step 3. Substituting $r=x-Px$ and $w=Px-y$ gives the displayed identity.

*Step 5: minimality and uniqueness.* In the identity, $\|x-Px\|^2$ does not depend on $y$, and $\|Px-y\|^2\ge 0$. Therefore, for every $y\in S$,

$$
\|x-y\|^2\ \ge\ \|x-Px\|^2 ,
$$

with equality when $y=Px$. So $Px$ attains the minimum, and $Px\in S$ by Step 1. If some $y\in S$ attains the same value, the identity gives $\|Px-y\|^2=0$, so $y=Px$. The minimizer is therefore unique. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Remarks.** The argument uses only $P^2=P$ and $P^T=P$. It does not use invertibility or rank of $P$. If $P=0$, then $S=\{0\}$, and the identity reads $\|x-0\|^2=\|x\|^2+\|0-0\|^2$, which holds. If $P$ is the identity matrix, then $S=\mathbb R^d$ and the residual $x-Px$ is zero. The result concerns squared distance to this fixed set $S$ only. It says nothing about other layout constraints.

$$

$$
be the set of permitted layout displacements. For every $x\in\mathbb R^d$ and every $y\in S$,
$$
\|x-y\|^2=\|x-Px\|^2+\|Px-y\|^2,
$$
where $\|v\|^2=v^Tv$. Consequently $Px$ is the unique element of $S$ minimizing $\|x-y\|^2$.

**Proof.** Fix $x\in\mathbb R^d$ and $y\in S$. Write
$$
r=x-Px,\qquad w=Px-y,
$$
so that $x-y=r+w$.

*Step 1: $P$ fixes $S$.* Taking $z=x$ shows $Px\in S$. Since $y\in S$, we have $y=Pz$ for some $z$, and idempotence gives
$$
Py=P^2z=Pz=y .
$$
The same applies to $Px$, so $P(Px)=Px$. By linearity,
$$
Pw=P(Px)-Py=Px-y=w .
$$

*Step 2: $Pr=0$.* Using $P^2=P$,
$$
Pr=Px-P^2x=Px-Px=0 .
$$

*Step 3: the cross term vanishes.* Since $w=Pw$ and $P^T=P$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
r^Tw
&= r^T(Pw) && \text{by Step 1}\\
&= (P^Tr)^Tw\\
&= (Pr)^Tw && \text{by symmetry, } P^T=P\\
&= 0 && \text{by Step 2.}
\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 4: the identity.* Expanding the squared norm of $x-y=r+w$,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\|x-y\|^2
&=(r+w)^T(r+w)\\
&=r^Tr+r^Tw+w^Tr+w^Tw\\
&=\|r\|^2+2\,r^Tw+\|w\|^2\\
&=\|r\|^2+\|w\|^2 ,
\end{aligned}
$$
where the third line uses $w^Tr=r^Tw$ (both are scalars) and the last line uses Step 3. This is
$$
\|x-y\|^2=\|x-Px\|^2+\|Px-y\|^2 .
$$

$$

$$

Now suppose some $y\in S$ also attains the minimum, so $\|x-y\|^2=\|x-Px\|^2$. The identity of Step 4 then gives $\|Px-y\|^2=0$. For a real vector $v$, $v^Tv=0$ only if $v=0$, so $y=Px$. Therefore the minimizer is unique. $\qquad\blacksquare$

- If $P=0$, then $S=\{0\}$ and $Px=0$. The identity reads $\|x\|^2=\|x\|^2+0$, and the only permitted displacement is $0$.

The result concerns squared Euclidean distance to this particular set $S$. It says nothing about other layout constraints.

response:
Focus lock keeps keyboard focus inside the current dialog until the dialog closes. It is useful when controls behind the dialog remain visible but should not receive keyboard input. Focus lock does not freeze the pointer, and it does not prevent the user from closing the dialog with the documented close command.

The implementation uses a sentinel at each end of the dialog's tab sequence. When focus reaches a sentinel, the handler moves it to the appropriate control at the opposite end. This is a focus-management mechanism, not a security boundary. Code running in the page can still move focus deliberately, so the application must handle those changes rather than assume the lock prevents them.

To test focus lock, open the dialog, traverse its controls in both directions, and close it while focus is on the last control. Focus should return to the control that opened the dialog. If that control has been removed, the application uses its documented fallback target. The fallback is part of the application's behavior and is not chosen by focus lock itself.

A separate hardware example describes a switch whose spring contacts latch when pressed. That use of latch refers to the physical mechanism. The example does not demonstrate the software feature and should not be used as a test of it.

Focus lock can help maintain a predictable keyboard sequence. It does not establish that labels, reading order, or announcements are correct; those require their own checks.

You will need the paper bridge, the tray, and the bag of counters from your group's box. Put the tray in the middle of the table and place the bridge across the tray. The bridge should rest on the two wooden blocks, not on the tray's rim. The tray is there to catch counters if they fall, so check that the tray sits under the middle of the bridge.

Before adding any counters, sketch the bridge from the side. Mark where the bridge touches the blocks. Then put one counter in the centre of the bridge and sketch the bridge again. Your second sketch should show the bridge, including any bend you can see, rather than just the new counter. If you cannot see a bend, say so beside the sketch.

Add counters one at a time, placing each on the same marked spot. After each addition, wait until the bridge stops moving before deciding whether to add another. The counters should stay in the tray if the bridge collapses. Do not rebuild the bridge during this first test, even if you have a promising idea about making it stronger.

When the test ends, count the counters that were on the bridge immediately before the bridge collapsed. If you stop because you have used all twelve counters and the bridge is still standing, record “held twelve; collapse not observed.” That is different from saying the bridge can hold exactly twelve.

Now discuss one change you would like to test next time. Keep your first sketches. These sketches record what this bridge did before the change, which will be useful when your next bridge behaves differently from the one you imagined.

# Tell us about one day's travel

We are asking households in the selected blocks to describe their travel on one ordinary day, including a day when nobody went anywhere. The survey is about trips, but a day with no trips is useful to us too. Some households have told us they assumed we didn't mean them because they mostly stay home. We do mean them.

## Which day to describe

The enclosed card gives your household a date. Please describe that date even if it was unusual for you. We assign the date so that the day comes from everyday life and is not one you choose to represent it.

If you can't remember when a trip began, an estimate is welcome, and the form has a box for marking estimates. If you can't remember whether a trip happened, please leave that part blank rather than filling in a likely trip.

## Who fills it out

One adult may complete the form for the household, checking with other members where possible. We ask how many people live in the household and their age bands. We do not ask for names.

## How your answers are handled

Your invitation carries a code so that we can stop reminders when your form arrives. The team that receives completed forms can see this code. The address list that links codes to homes will be deleted when reminders end, which is scheduled for the end of the following month. Until then, your responses are not anonymous.

Results will be published for groups of blocks, not for individual households.

## Taking part

Returning the form is voluntary. You may skip any question. An incomplete form stops reminders just as a complete one does.

We cannot remove a response after the address list has been deleted, because we will no longer be able to link a household's request to its form.

We hope you will help, including if your day's whole travel story is that you stayed put.

response:
We are asking households in the selected blocks to tell us about one ordinary day's travel. That includes days when nobody went anywhere. The survey is about trips, but a day with no trips is useful to us too. Some households have told us they assumed we didn't mean them because they mostly stay home. We do mean you.

**Filling out the form**

The enclosed card gives your household a date. Please describe that date even if it was unusual for you. We assign the date so that it comes from everyday life, not from a day you pick to represent it.

If you can't remember a trip's departure time, an estimate is welcome, and the form has a box for marking estimates. If you can't remember whether a trip happened, please leave that part blank rather than filling in a likely trip.

One adult may complete the form for the household, after checking with other members where possible. We ask how many people live in the household and their age bands, but not their names.

**Your invitation code and your privacy**

Your invitation has a code so that we can stop sending reminders once your form arrives. The team that receives completed forms can see this code. The address list that links codes to homes will be deleted after reminders finish, which is scheduled for the end of the following month. Until then, your responses are not anonymous.

Returning the form is voluntary. You may skip any question, and an incomplete form stops reminders just as a complete one does. Once the address list has been deleted, we cannot remove your response, because we will no longer be able to link a household's request to its form.

We will publish results for groups of blocks, not for individual households.

We hope you will take part, even if your day's whole travel story is that you stayed home.

The listening gallery offers two ways to hear the recorded accounts. You can use the fixed headphones beside each case, or borrow a receiver at the welcome desk to listen through the room’s induction loop. Receivers are free and do not need to be booked. We have six, so one may not be available immediately.

Every recording also has a printed transcript in the drawer beneath its case. The transcripts describe sounds that matter to the account, such as a bell or a pause interrupted by machinery, but not every background sound. Large-print copies are available at the welcome desk. You may take them into the gallery, but please return them before leaving.

At half past each hour, the room plays a three-minute sound sequence through its speakers. A light above the entrance comes on one minute before it begins. If you would rather avoid the sequence, you can leave through either doorway and return afterward. The recordings at the cases pause during the sequence, then resume from where they stopped.

On Wednesday mornings, from opening until noon, the speaker sequence is switched off. The case recordings and induction loop remain available. These mornings are quieter, but we cannot promise silence: people still talk, doors open, and school groups sometimes visit.

You are welcome to ask a gallery host for help with the equipment or for a seat. Hosts can explain the available options, though they cannot reserve a receiver or keep the room quiet for an individual visit. If you prefer to read before coming, you can request the same transcripts from the visitor team.

response:
Of the 600 households invited to our survey of library use, 360 returned the initial questionnaire. Among them, 252 reported using a library in the previous month, or 70 percent. The preliminary note reported this percentage for respondents, but subsequent discussion sometimes treated it as a figure for all 600 invited households.

We then attempted to contact the 240 initial nonrespondents by telephone. The budget covered 90 completed interviews, and interviewers stopped when they reached that total. These 90 households were not a simple random sample of the 240: inclusion depended on whether interviewers could reach them and whether they agreed to participate. Of those interviewed, 42 reported library use in the previous month, or approximately 46.7 percent.

Together, the two stages produced 294 reports of library use among 450 responding households, or approximately 65.3 percent. The decline from 70 to 65.3 percent shows how the observed result changed when the follow-up respondents were included. Their reported library use was lower than that of the initial respondents. Both stages used the same question and reference month, but households were not randomly assigned to respond by questionnaire or telephone. We therefore cannot separate differences in the people reached from any effect of the response mode.

The follow-up broadens the group we observed, but it does not establish the prevalence of library use among all 600 invited households. We still have no responses from 150 households and do not know whether they resemble either responding group. Claiming that the follow-up corrected for the remaining nonresponse would require assumptions that we have not evaluated. We used no weights and did not fill in missing responses.

The report should retain the results from both stages and present the combined 65.3 percent as a description of the 450 responding households. Alongside that figure, it should explain what remains unknown about the households that did not respond. response:
We started with the date field because it gave us an easy way to count completed entries. But a year entered in the index might not be supported by the card. An empty field could mean that the date was absent, that it could not be read, or that someone had overlooked it. Before counting completed fields, we needed to distinguish these cases.

We selected eighty catalogue cards from one drawer that had not yet been entered into the digital index. Two staff members transcribed each card independently. They could enter a year or mark the date as absent or unreadable. The instructions did not allow them to infer a year. A later joint inspection established a reference decision for each card. This gave us an internally reconciled record, not an independent external validation of the dates.

The reconciled record contained fifty cards with a readable year, eighteen with no date, and twelve with an unreadable date. The first transcriber entered the reference year on forty-seven of the fifty readable cards and marked three as unreadable. The second entered the reference year on forty-nine and marked one as unreadable. Neither entered a year on any of the thirty cards classified as absent or unreadable in the reconciled record. On those thirty cards, the transcribers agreed with each other about whether the date was absent or unreadable on twenty-six. We have not tabulated how often each transcriber agreed with the reconciled decision on that distinction.

Counting only cards with a year would make both transcribers’ work look substantially incomplete, even though the procedure required a different entry for cards with absent or unreadable dates. That count would also hide the four disagreements about why no year was entered. We need to keep these distinctions for later work. A reader trying to find a document’s date has a different question from a conservator deciding whether another imaging method might help.

We chose the drawer for convenience, so these counts describe the trial rather than estimate error across the collection. They suggest that we should report readable-year transcription separately from decisions about absent or unreadable dates. We have not tested whether this change would improve later retrieval.

response:
We should repeat the pond survey this season before describing the lower count as a population decline. Asking for another survey does not mean postponing action. It is an action we can take now to help interpret the lower count.

Last year’s team visited each of eight ponds twice at dusk. This year’s team visited the same ponds once at midday and recorded fewer animals in total. Neither visit frequency nor time of day has been accounted for, and the records do not contain enough information to reconstruct the missed dusk visits. We therefore know that the recorded total was lower, but we cannot read the size of a population change directly from the difference between the totals.

The lower count deserves attention because a drainage proposal concerns three of the surveyed ponds, and the advisory meeting is next month. Drainage has not begun, so the proposal does not explain the lower count. It does mean that the condition of the ponds matters to an upcoming decision. That timing makes further information more urgent, but it does not make the two surveys comparable.

We recommend two dusk visits to each pond using the earlier recording sheet. This would make the new observations more comparable with last year’s, although weather and detectability would still vary. The repeat survey would neither isolate the effect of drainage nor provide a population census. Its immediate purpose is to reduce an avoidable ambiguity in the evidence available to the meeting.

If the repeat survey cannot be completed before the meeting, the advisory note should report the lower observed total together with the differences in survey effort and timing. We can also report the planned work as pending. The current record supports neither a confident estimate of decline nor a confident assurance of stability. The monitoring request should be judged by whether it improves the upcoming decision, without requiring either conclusion in advance.

response:
We recommend keeping completed interviews in the weekly dashboard while ending the practice of ranking interviewers by that number alone. The count tells us whether fieldwork is moving, but it does not tell us enough to compare people whose assigned routes differ.

Some routes contain apartment buildings with a staffed entrance. Others contain scattered homes that require long walks between attempts. Assignments rotate each month, while the dashboard ranks interviewers each week. Rotation may spread difficult routes over a longer period without making any particular week's assignments comparable. We have not estimated how large that difference is.

The ranking also leaves out work that does not produce a completed interview. A careful refusal record or a return visit at the requested time may be necessary fieldwork even when no questionnaire results. Including those activities in the discussion would not mean treating every attempt as equally useful. Supervisors would still need to look at what happened and whether the agreed contact procedure was followed.

We do not propose replacing the ranking with a single weighted score. We have no tested weights, and a score could conceal the same judgment inside a formula. For the next four weeks, the dashboard should show completed interviews, attempts, and route assignments together, with supervisors adding a brief explanation when discussing unusual totals.

This arrangement will take more attention than reading a league table, and that cost is part of the recommendation. It may also reveal problems that the old ranking missed, but we cannot claim that it will improve response rates before trying it. At the end of four weeks, the steering group should ask whether the added context helped supervisors make useful decisions and whether the burden was manageable. The aim is to make the weekly discussion more informative while preserving a clear view of fieldwork progress.

response:
We recommend keeping completed interviews in the weekly dashboard and ending the practice of ranking interviewers by that number alone. The count tells us whether fieldwork is moving, but it does not tell us enough to compare people whose assigned routes differ.

Some routes contain apartment buildings with a staffed entrance. Others contain scattered homes that require long walks between attempts. Assignments rotate each month, but the dashboard ranks interviewers each week. Rotation may spread difficult routes over a longer period, but it does not make any particular week's assignments comparable. We have not estimated how large that difference is.

The ranking also leaves out work that does not produce a completed interview. A careful refusal record or a return visit at the requested time may be necessary fieldwork even when no questionnaire results. Counting those activities would not mean treating every attempt as equally useful. Supervisors would still need to look at what happened and whether the agreed contact procedure was followed.

We do not propose replacing the ranking with a single weighted score. We have no tested weights, and a score could hide the same judgment inside a formula. For the next four weeks, the dashboard should show completed interviews, attempts, and route assignments together, and supervisors should add a brief explanation when discussing unusual totals.

This arrangement will take more attention than reading a league table, and that cost is part of the recommendation. It may also reveal problems the old ranking missed, but we cannot claim it will improve response rates before trying it. At the end of four weeks, the steering group should ask whether the added context changed useful supervisory decisions and whether the burden was manageable. The aim is to make the weekly discussion more informative while keeping a clear view of fieldwork progress.

response:
Let \(N\geq 2\), and let \(y_1,\ldots,y_N\) be fixed real responses. Write
\[
\mu=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N y_i,
\qquad
\sigma^2=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N(y_i-\mu)^2.
\]
Choose an unordered pair \(P\) uniformly from the \(\binom{N}{2}\) pairs, then choose \(J\) uniformly from the two indices in \(P\). Set
\[
Y=y_J,
\qquad
Z=\frac12\sum_{i\in P}y_i.
\]
We will show that
\[
\mathbb E[Z]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2.
\]
All expectations and variances refer to repeated sampling from this fixed population.

Conditional on \(P=\{i,j\}\), the variable \(Y\) takes the values \(y_i\) and \(y_j\), each with probability \(1/2\). Hence
\[
\mathbb E[Y\mid P=\{i,j\}]
=\frac{y_i+y_j}{2},
\]
so \(\mathbb E[Y\mid P]=Z\). Each index belongs to \(N-1\) pairs, and therefore, for every \(i\),
\[
\Pr(J=i)
=\sum_{j\ne i}\Pr(P=\{i,j\})\Pr(J=i\mid P=\{i,j\})
=\frac{N-1}{2\binom{N}{2}}
=\frac1N.
\]
Thus
\[
\mathbb E[Y]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\sigma^2.
\]
Averaging the conditional mean gives
\[
\mathbb E[Z]
=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[Y\mid P]\right]
=\mathbb E[Y]
=\mu.
\]

To relate the two variances, write
\[
Y-\mu=(Y-Z)+(Z-\mu).
\]
Because \(Z\) is determined by \(P\),
\[
\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]
=\mathbb E[Y\mid P]-Z
=0.
\]
The same conditioning allows us to take \(Z-\mu\) outside the conditional expectation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)]
&=\mathbb E\!\left[\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)\mid P]\right]\\
&=\mathbb E\!\left[(Z-\mu)\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]\right]\\
&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Expanding the square now yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2
&=\mathbb E[(Y-\mu)^2]\\
&=\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]
  +2\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)]
  +\mathbb E[(Z-\mu)^2]\\
&=\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]+\operatorname{Var}(Z).
\end{aligned}
\]
The mixed term vanishes by conditional expectation. This is an orthogonality relation and does not require \(Y\) and \(Z\) to be independent.

It remains to compute \(\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]\). Given \(P=\{i,j\}\), the difference \(Y-Z\) equals either \((y_i-y_j)/2\) or its negative. Thus
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2\mid P=\{i,j\}]
=\frac{(y_i-y_j)^2}{4}.
\]
To average over pairs, we use the finite identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2
&=(N-1)\sum_{i=1}^N y_i^2-2\sum_{i<j}y_i y_j\\
&=N\sum_{i=1}^N y_i^2-\left(\sum_{i=1}^N y_i\right)^2\\
&=N\left(\sum_{i=1}^N y_i^2-N\mu^2\right)\\
&=N\sum_{i=1}^N(y_i-\mu)^2\\
&=N^2\sigma^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
The first equality counts each \(y_i^2\) in \(N-1\) pairs, and the second expands the square of the sum. Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]
&=\frac{1}{\binom{N}{2}}\sum_{i<j}\frac{(y_i-y_j)^2}{4}\\
&=\frac{N^2\sigma^2}{4\binom{N}{2}}\\
&=\frac{N}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Substituting into the variance decomposition gives
\[
\operatorname{Var}(Z)
=\sigma^2-\frac{N}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2
=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2.
\]

When \(N=2\), the sampled pair is the full population, so \(Z=\mu\) is constant. If all responses coincide, both variances vanish for every \(N\). The argument requires no division by \(\sigma^2\).

response:
**Proposition.** Let $N\ge 2$ and let $y_1,\dots,y_N$ be fixed real numbers. Define

$$
\mu=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N y_i,\qquad \sigma^2=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N (y_i-\mu)^2.
$$

Choose an unordered pair $P$ of distinct indices uniformly from the $\binom N2$ pairs. Given $P$, choose $J$ uniformly from the two indices in $P$. Set

$$
Y=y_J,\qquad Z=\frac12\sum_{i\in P} y_i.
$$

Then $\mathbb E[Z]=\mu$ and

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\,\sigma^2.
$$

The randomness comes only from the sampling design. The responses $y_i$ are fixed, so this is repeated sampling from a fixed population, not uncertainty in the responses.

**Proof.**

**Step 1: Conditional moments given $P$.** Fix a pair $P=\{i,j\}$. Given $P$, $J$ equals $i$ or $j$ with probability $1/2$ each. Since $Z$ is a function of $P$, it is fixed once $P$ is known. Therefore

$$
\mathbb E[Y\mid P]=\frac{y_i+y_j}{2}=Z.
$$

Also, $Y-Z$ equals $(y_i-y_j)/2$ when $J=i$ and $(y_j-y_i)/2$ when $J=j$. In both cases the square is $(y_i-y_j)^2/4$, so

$$
\mathbb E\big[(Y-Z)^2\mid P=\{i,j\}\big]=\frac{(y_i-y_j)^2}{4}.
$$

**Step 2: The marginal law of $J$.** Each index $i$ belongs to exactly $N-1$ of the $\binom N2$ pairs. Given such a pair, $J=i$ with probability $1/2$. Hence

$$
\Pr(J=i)=\sum_{P\ni i}\Pr(P)\,\Pr(J=i\mid P)
=\frac{N-1}{\binom N2}\cdot\frac12
=\frac{2}{N}\cdot\frac12=\frac1N.
$$

So $J$ is uniform on $\{1,\dots,N\}$. It follows that

$$
\mathbb E[Y]=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N y_i=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N(y_i-\mu)^2=\sigma^2.
$$

**Step 3: $\mathbb E[Z]=\mu$.** By the tower property and Step 1,

$$
\mathbb E[Z]=\mathbb E\big[\mathbb E[Y\mid P]\big]=\mathbb E[Y]=\mu.
$$

**Step 4: Orthogonality.** Write $Y-\mu=(Y-Z)+(Z-\mu)$ and expand the square:

$$
\sigma^2=\mathbb E[(Y-\mu)^2]
=\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]+2\,\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)]+\mathbb E[(Z-\mu)^2].
$$

The cross term is zero. The factor $Z-\mu$ is a function of $P$, so it can be moved outside the conditional expectation given $P$:

$$
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)]
=\mathbb E\Big[(Z-\mu)\,\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]\Big].
$$

By Step 1, $\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]=\mathbb E[Y\mid P]-Z=0$, so the cross term vanishes.

This argument uses only that $Z-\mu$ is determined by $P$ and that $\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]=0$. It does not require $Y$ and $Z$ to be independent. By Step 3, $\mathbb E[(Z-\mu)^2]=\operatorname{Var}(Z)$, so

$$
\sigma^2=\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]+\operatorname{Var}(Z). \tag{1}
$$

**Step 5: A pairwise identity.** The summand $(y_i-y_j)^2$ is symmetric in $i$ and $j$, and its diagonal terms $i=j$ are zero. So we may sum over all ordered pairs and halve:

$$
\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2
=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^N\big(y_i^2-2y_iy_j+y_j^2\big).
$$

Write $S_1=\sum_i y_i$ and $S_2=\sum_i y_i^2$. Then

$$
\frac12\Big(NS_2-2S_1^2+NS_2\Big)=NS_2-S_1^2.
$$

Since $S_1=N\mu$ and $\sum_i(y_i-\mu)^2=S_2-N\mu^2$,

$$
NS_2-S_1^2=N\big(S_2-N\mu^2\big)=N\sum_i(y_i-\mu)^2=N^2\sigma^2.
$$

Thus

$$
\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2=N^2\sigma^2. \tag{2}
$$

**Step 6: Computing $\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]$.** Average the conditional second moment from Step 1 over the uniform choice of $P$, then apply (2):

$$
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]
=\frac{1}{\binom N2}\sum_{i<j}\frac{(y_i-y_j)^2}{4}
=\frac{N^2\sigma^2}{4\cdot\frac{N(N-1)}{2}}
=\frac{N\sigma^2}{2(N-1)}.
$$

**Step 7: Conclusion.** Substitute Step 6 into (1):

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\sigma^2-\frac{N\sigma^2}{2(N-1)}
=\sigma^2\,\frac{2(N-1)-N}{2(N-1)}
=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\,\sigma^2. \qquad\blacksquare
$$

**Remarks.** The proof never divides by $\sigma^2$, so no separate case is needed when $\sigma^2=0$. In that case all $y_i$ are equal, and both $\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Z)$ are zero, consistent with the formulas. When $N=2$, the only pair is the whole population, so $P$ is fixed and $Z=(y_1+y_2)/2=\mu$ is constant. The formula gives $\operatorname{Var}(Z)=0$, which agrees.

**Setup.** Let $N \ge 2$, and let $y_1,\dots,y_N$ be fixed real responses with
$$
\mu = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N y_i,\qquad \sigma^2 = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N (y_i-\mu)^2.
$$
The randomness comes from the sampling design, not from the responses. The unordered pair $P$ is uniform over the $\binom{N}{2}$ pairs, and given $P$, the index $J$ is uniform over the two indices in $P$. Set
$$
Y = y_J,\qquad Z = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i\in P} y_i.
$$
$Z$ is a function of $P$ alone, so $Z$ is fixed once $P$ is known.

**Step 1: Conditional moments given $P$.** Fix a pair $P=\{i,j\}$. Then $J=i$ or $J=j$, each with probability $\tfrac12$. Therefore
$$
E[Y\mid P] = \frac{y_i+y_j}{2} = Z.
$$
Also, $Y-Z$ equals $\tfrac12(y_i-y_j)$ when $J=i$ and $-\tfrac12(y_i-y_j)$ when $J=j$. Each occurs with probability $\tfrac12$, so
$$
E\big[(Y-Z)^2 \mid P=\{i,j\}\big] = \frac{(y_i-y_j)^2}{4}.
$$
These two conditional facts are the only properties of the conditional distribution used below. No independence between $Y$ and $Z$ is assumed.

**Step 2: Marginal moments of $Y$.** Each index $i$ belongs to $N-1$ pairs. Hence
$$
P(J=i) = \sum_{j\ne i}\frac{1}{\binom{N}{2}}\cdot\frac12 = \frac{N-1}{2\binom{N}{2}} = \frac{1}{N}.
$$
So $J$ is uniform on $\{1,\dots,N\}$, and
$$
E[Y] = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N y_i = \mu,\qquad E[Y^2] = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N y_i^2.
$$
Thus $\operatorname{Var}(Y) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i y_i^2 - \mu^2 = \sigma^2$. Averaging Step 1 over $P$ gives
$$
E[Z] = E\big[E[Y\mid P]\big] = E[Y] = \mu.
$$

**Step 3: Orthogonality.** Write $Y-\mu = (Y-Z)+(Z-\mu)$ and square:
$$
\sigma^2 = E[(Y-\mu)^2] = E[(Y-Z)^2] + 2\,E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)] + E[(Z-\mu)^2].
$$
The cross term vanishes. Since $Z-\mu$ is a function of $P$, it can be taken outside the conditional expectation given $P$:
$$
E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)] = E\Big[(Z-\mu)\,E[Y-Z\mid P]\Big] = 0,
$$
because $E[Y-Z\mid P]=0$ by Step 1. Since $E[Z]=\mu$, we have $E[(Z-\mu)^2] = \operatorname{Var}(Z)$. Therefore
$$
\sigma^2 = E[(Y-Z)^2] + \operatorname{Var}(Z).
$$

**Step 4: Computing $E[(Y-Z)^2]$.** Averaging the conditional second moment over the uniform pair $P$ gives
$$
E[(Y-Z)^2] = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{2}}\sum_{i<j}\frac{(y_i-y_j)^2}{4}.
$$
To evaluate the pair sum, expand the square over all ordered pairs:
$$
\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2 = \frac12\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^N (y_i-y_j)^2 = N\sum_{i=1}^N y_i^2 - \Big(\sum_{i=1}^N y_i\Big)^2.
$$
Now substitute $\sum_i y_i^2 = N(\sigma^2+\mu^2)$ and $\sum_i y_i = N\mu$:
$$
N\sum_i y_i^2 - \Big(\sum_i y_i\Big)^2 = N^2(\sigma^2+\mu^2) - N^2\mu^2 = N^2\sigma^2.
$$
Since $4\binom{N}{2} = 2N(N-1)$,
$$
E[(Y-Z)^2] = \frac{N^2\sigma^2}{2N(N-1)} = \frac{N\sigma^2}{2(N-1)}.
$$

**Step 5: Conclusion.** Subtracting from Step 3,
$$
\operatorname{Var}(Z) = \sigma^2 - \frac{N\sigma^2}{2(N-1)} = \frac{2(N-1)-N}{2(N-1)}\,\sigma^2 = \frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\,\sigma^2.
$$

When $N=2$, the only pair is the whole population, so $Z=\mu$ is constant and the formula gives $\operatorname{Var}(Z)=0$. If all $y_i$ are equal, then $\sigma^2=0$, and every quantity above vanishes. The argument never divides by $\sigma^2$, so this case needs no separate treatment.

Let \(N\ge 2\), and let \(y_1,\ldots,y_N\) be fixed real responses. Define
\[
\mu=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N y_i,
\qquad
\sigma^2=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N(y_i-\mu)^2.
\]
Choose an unordered pair \(P\) uniformly from the \(\binom{N}{2}\) pairs, then choose \(J\) uniformly from the two indices in \(P\). Set
\[
Y=y_J,
\qquad
Z=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i\in P}y_i.
\]
Then
\[
\mathbb E[Z]=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2.
\]
These variances describe repeated sampling from the fixed population; the responses themselves are not random.

Given \(P=\{i,j\}\), the index \(J\) is equally likely to be \(i\) or \(j\). Therefore,
\[
\mathbb E[Y\mid P=\{i,j\}]
=\frac{y_i+y_j}{2}
=Z,
\]
and
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2\mid P=\{i,j\}]
=\frac{(y_i-y_j)^2}{4}.
\]
Each index occurs in \(N-1\) pairs, so \(J\) is uniform over all \(N\) indices. Hence \(\mathbb E[Y]=\mu\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\sigma^2\). Taking expectations in \(\mathbb E[Y\mid P]=Z\) gives \(\mathbb E[Z]=\mu\).

To relate the two variances, write \(Y-\mu=(Y-Z)+(Z-\mu)\). Since \(Z-\mu\) is determined by \(P\), conditional expectation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)]
&=\mathbb E\!\left[(Z-\mu)\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]\right]\\
&=0,
\end{aligned}
\]
because \(\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]=0\). Thus the cross term vanishes when we expand the square:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2
=\operatorname{Var}(Y)
&=\mathbb E[(Y-\mu)^2]\\
&=\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]+\mathbb E[(Z-\mu)^2]\\
&=\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]+\operatorname{Var}(Z).
\end{aligned}
\]
This uses the conditional mean of \(Y-Z\), not independence of \(Y\) and \(Z\).

The sum of squared pairwise differences satisfies
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2
&=N\sum_i y_i^2-\left(\sum_i y_i\right)^2\\
&=N\sum_i(y_i-\mu)^2\\
&=N^2\sigma^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Averaging the conditional squared deviations over the uniformly chosen pair therefore yields
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]
=\frac{1}{4\binom{N}{2}}\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2
=\frac{N\sigma^2}{2(N-1)}.
\]
Subtracting this from \(\sigma^2\) gives
\[
\operatorname{Var}(Z)
=\sigma^2-\frac{N\sigma^2}{2(N-1)}
=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2.
\]
When \(N=2\), the pair is the full population and \(Z\) is constant. If all responses coincide, both variances are zero for every \(N\); the derivation does not divide by \(\sigma^2\).

$$
Y=y_J,\qquad Z=\frac12\sum_{i\in P}y_i .
$$
Then
$$
\mathbb E[Z]=\mu,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\,\sigma^2 .
$$

$$
\mathbb E[Y\mid P]=\frac{y_i+y_j}{2}=Z,

$$
\mathbb E\big[(Y-Z)^2\mid P=\{i,j\}\big]=\frac{(y_i-y_j)^2}{4}.

$$
\mathbb P(J=i)=\frac{N-1}{\binom N2}\cdot\frac12=\frac{N-1}{N(N-1)/2}\cdot\frac12=\frac1N .
$$
Thus $J$ is uniform on $\{1,\dots,N\}$, and therefore
$$
\mathbb E[Y]=\mu,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y)=\sigma^2 .
$$
Taking expectations in $\mathbb E[Y\mid P]=Z$ gives $\mathbb E[Z]=\mathbb E[Y]=\mu$.

**Step 3: Decomposition of $\sigma^2$.** Write $Y-\mu=(Y-Z)+(Z-\mu)$ and expand the square:
$$
\sigma^2=\mathbb E[(Y-\mu)^2]
=\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]+2\,\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)]+\mathbb E[(Z-\mu)^2].
$$
The last term is $\operatorname{Var}(Z)$ because $\mathbb E[Z]=\mu$. For the cross term, $Z$ is a function of $P$, so $Z-\mu$ can be taken outside the conditional expectation given $P$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)]
&=\mathbb E\Big[\mathbb E\big[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)\mid P\big]\Big]\\
&=\mathbb E\Big[(Z-\mu)\,\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]\Big]\\
&=0,
\end{aligned}
$$
where the last equality uses $\mathbb E[Y\mid P]=Z$ from Step 1. This argument uses only that $Z$ is determined by $P$. It does not assume that $Y$ and $Z$ are independent, and they are not. We conclude
$$
\sigma^2=\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]+\operatorname{Var}(Z). \tag{1}
$$

**Step 4: The term $\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]$.** Since $P$ is uniform over the $\binom N2$ pairs, Step 1 gives
$$
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]
=\frac{1}{\binom N2}\sum_{i<j}\frac{(y_i-y_j)^2}{4}.
$$
To evaluate the sum, note that the ordered double sum counts each unordered pair twice and has zero diagonal terms:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2
&=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^N (y_i-y_j)^2\\
&=\frac12\Big(2N\sum_i y_i^2-2\Big(\sum_i y_i\Big)^2\Big)\\
&=N\sum_i y_i^2-\Big(\sum_i y_i\Big)^2\\
&=N\sum_i (y_i-\mu)^2\\
&=N^2\sigma^2 .
\end{aligned}
$$
The fourth line uses $\sum_i(y_i-\mu)^2=\sum_i y_i^2-N\mu^2=\sum_i y_i^2-\frac1N\big(\sum_i y_i\big)^2$. Since $4\binom N2=2N(N-1)$,
$$
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]=\frac{N^2\sigma^2}{2N(N-1)}=\frac{N}{2(N-1)}\,\sigma^2 .
$$

**Step 5: Conclusion.** Substituting into (1) and subtracting,
$$
\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\sigma^2-\frac{N}{2(N-1)}\sigma^2
=\frac{2(N-1)-N}{2(N-1)}\,\sigma^2
=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\,\sigma^2 .
$$

**Edge cases.** For $N=2$ the only pair is the whole population, so $Z=\mu$ is constant, which agrees with the formula's value $0$. If all responses are equal, then $\sigma^2=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Z)=0$ for every $N$. The argument never divides by $\sigma^2$, so these cases need no separate treatment. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Setup.** Let $N\ge 2$ and let $y_1,\dots,y_N$ be fixed real responses. Write
$$
\mu=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N y_i,\qquad \sigma^2=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N (y_i-\mu)^2 .
$$
Choose an unordered pair $P$ uniformly from the $\binom N2$ pairs, then choose $J$ uniformly from the two indices in $P$. Set
$$
Y=y_J,\qquad Z=\frac12\sum_{i\in P} y_i .
$$
We show that
$$
\mathbb E[Z]=\mu,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Z)=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\,\sigma^2 .
$$
All expectations and variances are over the random choice of $P$ and $J$ for the fixed population. The responses themselves are not random.

**Step 1: conditional behavior of $Y$.** Given $P=\{i,j\}$, $Y$ equals $y_i$ or $y_j$ with probability $1/2$ each, and $Z=(y_i+y_j)/2$. Hence
$$
\mathbb E[Y\mid P]=Z,
$$
and since $Y-Z=\pm (y_i-y_j)/2$ in either case,
$$
\mathbb E\big[(Y-Z)^2\mid P=\{i,j\}\big]=\frac{(y_i-y_j)^2}{4}.
$$

**Step 2: the marginal law of $Y$ and the mean of $Z$.** Each index $k$ lies in exactly $N-1$ pairs, and given such a pair, $J=k$ with probability $1/2$. Therefore
$$
\Pr(J=k)=\frac{N-1}{\binom N2}\cdot\frac12=\frac1N ,
$$
so $J$ is uniform on $\{1,\dots,N\}$. It follows that $\mathbb E[Y]=\mu$ and $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mathbb E[(Y-\mu)^2]=\sigma^2$. Taking expectations in $\mathbb E[Y\mid P]=Z$ gives
$$
\mathbb E[Z]=\mathbb E[Y]=\mu .
$$

**Step 3: decomposition of $\sigma^2$.** Write $Y-\mu=(Y-Z)+(Z-\mu)$ and expand the square:
$$
\sigma^2=\mathbb E[(Y-\mu)^2]
=\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]+2\,\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)]+\mathbb E[(Z-\mu)^2].
$$
The last term is $\operatorname{Var}(Z)$ because $\mathbb E[Z]=\mu$. For the cross term, $Z$ is a function of $P$, so $Z-\mu$ can be taken outside the conditional expectation given $P$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)]
&=\mathbb E\Big[\mathbb E\big[(Y-Z)(Z-\mu)\mid P\big]\Big]\\
&=\mathbb E\Big[(Z-\mu)\,\mathbb E[Y-Z\mid P]\Big]\\
&=0,
\end{aligned}
$$
where the last equality uses $\mathbb E[Y\mid P]=Z$ from Step 1. This argument uses only that $Z$ is determined by $P$ and that $Y$ has conditional mean $Z$ given $P$. It does not require $Y$ and $Z$ to be independent, and in general they are not. We conclude
$$
\sigma^2=\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]+\operatorname{Var}(Z). \tag{1}
$$

**Step 4: the term $\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]$.** Averaging the conditional second moment from Step 1 over the $\binom N2$ equally likely pairs gives
$$
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]=\frac{1}{\binom N2}\sum_{i<j}\frac{(y_i-y_j)^2}{4}.
$$
For the sum, expanding the squares gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i<j}(y_i-y_j)^2
&=N\sum_{i}y_i^2-\Big(\sum_i y_i\Big)^2\\
&=N\Big(\sum_i y_i^2-N\mu^2\Big)\\
&=N\sum_i (y_i-\mu)^2\\
&=N^2\sigma^2 .
\end{aligned}
$$
Since $\binom N2=N(N-1)/2$,
$$
\mathbb E[(Y-Z)^2]=\frac{N^2\sigma^2}{4\binom N2}=\frac{N\sigma^2}{2(N-1)} .
$$

**Step 5: conclusion.** Substituting into (1),
$$
\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\sigma^2-\frac{N\sigma^2}{2(N-1)}
=\frac{2(N-1)-N}{2(N-1)}\,\sigma^2
=\frac{N-2}{2(N-1)}\,\sigma^2 .
$$

**Special cases.** When $N=2$ there is only one pair, which is the whole population, so $Z=\mu$ is constant and the formula gives $\operatorname{Var}(Z)=0$. If all responses coincide, then $\sigma^2=0$ and every variance above is $0$ for every $N$. The argument never divides by $\sigma^2$, so this case needs no separate treatment.

Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{r\times d}\) and \(y=Ax+e\), where \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), \(e\in\mathbb R^r\), and \(\|e\|_2\leq\varepsilon\) for \(\varepsilon\geq0\). Set \(K=\ker A\), and let \(P\) be the orthogonal projection onto \(K^\perp\). Suppose \(\gamma>0\) and
\[
\|Av\|_2\geq\gamma\|v\|_2
\qquad\text{for every }v\in K^\perp.
\]
For any least-squares minimizer \(\hat x\) of \(\|Az-y\|_2\), which exists in finite dimensions, we claim that
\[
\|P(\hat x-x)\|_2\leq\frac{\varepsilon}{\gamma}.
\]

To prove this, put \(h=\hat x-x\). The normal equations and \(y=Ax+e\) give
\[
A^\top(A\hat x-y)=0,
\qquad
A^\top(Ah-e)=0.
\]
Multiplying the second identity by \(h^\top\) and applying the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality yields
\[
\|Ah\|_2^2
=\langle Ah,e\rangle
\leq\|Ah\|_2\|e\|_2
\leq\varepsilon\|Ah\|_2.
\]
If \(Ah\neq0\), division by \(\|Ah\|_2\) gives \(\|Ah\|_2\leq\varepsilon\). The same bound holds when \(Ah=0\).

We now decompose the error orthogonally:
\[
h=Ph+(I-P)h,
\qquad
Ph\in K^\perp,\quad (I-P)h\in K.
\]
Since \(A\) vanishes on \(K\),
\[
Ah=APh+A(I-P)h=APh.
\]
Applying the assumed lower bound to \(Ph\) therefore gives
\[
\gamma\|Ph\|_2
\leq\|APh\|_2
=\|Ah\|_2
\leq\varepsilon.
\]
Dividing by \(\gamma>0\) proves the claim.

When \(\varepsilon=0\), this shows \(P\hat x=Px\), so the observable component is recovered exactly. It does not imply uniqueness of \(\hat x\), since adding any vector in \(K\) leaves the least-squares objective unchanged. If \(K^\perp=\{0\}\), then \(P=0\) and the claimed bound holds trivially. No bound on the error component in \(K\) follows from these assumptions.

$$
\|P(\hat x-x)\|_2\le \frac{\varepsilon}{\gamma}.
$$

**Proof.** Put $h=\hat x-x$. Since $\hat x$ minimizes $\|Az-y\|_2$, the normal equations give $A^\top(A\hat x-y)=0$. Because $y=Ax+e$, we have $A\hat x-y=Ah-e$, so
$$
A^\top(Ah-e)=0. \tag{1}
$$

$$
\|Ah\|_2^2=\langle Ah,e\rangle\le \|Ah\|_2\,\|e\|_2\le \varepsilon\,\|Ah\|_2.
$$
If $\|Ah\|_2>0$, dividing by $\|Ah\|_2$ gives $\|Ah\|_2\le\varepsilon$. If $\|Ah\|_2=0$, then $\|Ah\|_2\le\varepsilon$ holds because $\varepsilon\ge 0$. In either case
$$
\|Ah\|_2\le \varepsilon. \tag{2}
$$

*Step 2: remove the component in $K$.* Let $Q=I-P$, the orthogonal projection onto $K$. Then
$$
h=Ph+Qh,\qquad Ph\in K^\perp,\qquad Qh\in K.
$$
Since $Qh\in K=\{v: Av=0\}$, we have $AQh=0$, and therefore
$$
Ah=A(Ph)+A(Qh)=A(Ph). \tag{3}
$$
The component $Qh$ drops out of $Ah$ entirely, so the unknown part of the error does not affect the bound.

*Step 3: apply the lower bound to $Ph$.* Since $Ph\in K^\perp$, the hypothesis applies to $v=Ph$:
$$
\gamma\|Ph\|_2\le \|A(Ph)\|_2=\|Ah\|_2\le \varepsilon,
$$
where the equality is (3) and the last inequality is (2). Dividing by $\gamma>0$ gives
$$
\|P(\hat x-x)\|_2=\|Ph\|_2\le \frac{\varepsilon}{\gamma}.
$$
$\blacksquare$

- If $K^\perp=\{0\}$, then $P=0$ and the claim is trivial. The argument above also covers this case, since $Ph=0$.
- If $\varepsilon=0$, then (2) gives $Ah=0$, and Step 3 gives $Ph=0$. So $A\hat x=Ax$ and $P\hat x=Px$, which means the observable component is recovered exactly. The argument does not show that $\hat x=x$ or that the minimizer is unique. Those conclusions would require information about $Qh$, which the hypotheses do not supply.
